Hanukkah. The Festival of Lights is an eight-day celebration beginning on the twenty-fifth day of Kislev, falling in November or December. It commemorates the rededication of the Second Temple following the Maccabean revolt against Greek-Syrian rule in the second century BCE, celebrating Jewish religious freedom and the triumph of a small resistance movement against a powerful empire.

The menorah, an eight-branched candelabrum, is lit each night with one additional candle lit each successive evening, symbolizing increasing light and hope. A hanukkiah, the Hanukkah menorah, has nine branches—eight for the holiday nights and one for the shamash, a helper candle used to light the others. The spiritual core of the holiday is the miracle of the oil, that one day's worth of oil burned for eight days in the rededicated Temple.

Dreidels, four-sided spinning tops bearing Hebrew letters, are played as games, a tradition originating from the period when Jewish study was forbidden. Traditional foods include latkes, fried potato pancakes, and sufganiyot, jelly-filled donuts, celebrating the oil's role in both the miracle and the holiday's cuisine.

The holiday is relatively minor in traditional Jewish law but has become culturally significant, partly due to its proximity to Christmas. Hanukkah is not a biblical holiday; it was established by the rabbis to commemorate events recorded in the Books of Maccabees. Unlike most Jewish holidays, there is no prohibition on work or school during Hanukkah in traditional observance. The holiday celebrates the Maccabees, the Jewish resistance movement whose victory it honors, and the Second Temple, whose rededication is the historical basis for this celebration of Jewish religious autonomy and identity.
